result.summary: Modify `node::GetTransaction` and `TxIndex` methods to throw `std::runtime_error` on block data I/O failures, deserialization errors, and index corruption instead of treating them as missing transactions. Update `getrawtransaction` to call `CheckBlockDataAvailability` on errors to provide explicit error messages for pruned or downloading blocks, and consolidate `ProcessPSBT` lookups to use `GetTransaction` directly.
result.problem: When disk reads fail due to I/O errors, block file corruption, or index database corruption, `GetTransaction` and `TxIndex` return null or empty results. Callers like `getrawtransaction`, `gettxoutproof`, and `/rest/tx/` misinterpret this as a nonexistent transaction and report it as missing, misleading users and masking disk corruption.
evidence: Commit `fad44f18b8`: 'When a block hash is passed in and the block can't be read, the RPC reports "No such transaction found in the provided block", even though the block was never searched. Fix this by throwing an I/O error from GetTransaction when ReadBlock fails.'
Commit `fa12509a47`: '...a -txindex corruption may also point to a larger system corruption and it seems better to notify the user properly by throwing an exception.'
result.changed_since_previous: Added release notes in doc/release-notes-35728.md detailing the changed error behavior for getrawtransaction, gettxoutproof, utxoupdatepsbt, descriptorprocesspsbt, and /rest/tx/.
result.card: TxIndex and node::GetTransaction now throw std::runtime_error on disk I/O, deserialization, and index corruption failures rather than returning null. Currently, disk read errors or txindex corruption lead RPC and REST callers to report confirmed transactions as missing, concealing disk failure or corruption. This change causes endpoints such as getrawtransaction, gettxoutproof, PSBT processors, and /rest/tx/ to return internal errors instead of false 'not found' responses, while distinguishing pruned or downloading blocks with CheckBlockDataAvailability.

risk.why: Uncaught exceptions or unexpected error paths could crash the node process or disrupt RPC clients expecting standard JSON-RPC error codes.
